newsitem.title: USA: U.S. budget leaders wind down talks with optimism.
newsitem.headline: U.S. budget leaders wind down talks with optimism.

text.p: The White House and Congress wound down budget negotiations Wednesday with no handshakes on a balanced budget agreement but there was talk of progress and hope the effort would resume next week.
Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican who had called this the "make it or break it" week for the budget, said he felt the talks did "make it."

"Essentially, I remain positive. I still think the issues that separate us are very big, very important. But I am willing to say come next week we are apt to be finished and we are apt to get a budget," he said at the end of the day's bargaining session.

After 10 days of meetings in Domenici's hideaway office, the negotiators said they will take a break until at least Wednesday to assess the progress separately. One more brief session will be held Thursday to discuss foreign affairs.
White House budget chief Frank Raines told reporters the next step was to take stock of the talks so far and he expected more negotiations next week.
"I think we are 'making.' I think we have met Sen. Domenici's test. We are in the process of making an agreement," he told reporters.

"As the process has gone on, they have found that the president's budget has many features to it that they can find agreeable. We are very happy about that," Raines said. "We hope to find more and more so that we can have a final agreement."

While, as Democratic Representative John Spratt of South Carolina said, there was "no sabre rattling" in the talks Wednesday, the negotiators did not make enough progress to take a final plan to the House and Senate leadership and to President Clinton.
A meeting at the White House had been penciled in for Wednesday, and then shifted to Friday. But a congressional aide said the meeting could occur next week.

"The Democrats and the White House are beginning to understand what we need and I believe they are doing some good in coming our way on some of them. We are beginning to understand some of their concerns," said Domenici.

But his House counterpart, Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich took a harder line. Over the last couple of days the Ohio Republican has had a series of what he called "listening sessions" with various groups within the party.

Kasich faces the difficult task of pleasing two major party factions -- conservatives who are adamant that a balanced budget agreement must include a sizeable tax cut and moderates who would prefer the budget deficit be brought to zero before taxes are reduced.
"Our position is we don't want any new programmes. We don't want any new spending," Kasich said.
But Kasich said his comments should not be seen as pessimism on the chances of reaching a deal. The next step would be discussions on where each side could give up some of its goals.

On one of the major sticking points in the talks, Medicare health care spending, Raines said the White House was sticking by its offer of an additional $18 billion in reductions, which which brought the total to $100 billion over five years.
"We believe that is a very good proposal and that is our proposal," he said.
